opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is a scenario I think about a lot, because I think it's actually pretty plausible. You might end up in a world where the AI company as a whole isn't very invested in safety. Maybe leadership is racing, maybe they're only willing to spend a small fraction of their compute on safety. But there's a small group of people inside who really care and who have some resources and some political capital. The question is what they should do with that.

The first thing I'd say is that ten people is actually enough to do a surprising amount, if they prioritize ruthlessly. You're not trying to solve alignment in that scenario. You're trying to pick the interventions that are cheap, that don't need buy-in from the whole organization, and that buy you a lot of risk reduction per unit of effort.

A big category there is what I'd call control: assume the models might be scheming against you, and try to set things up so that even if they are, they can't cause a catastrophe. Concretely, the thing I'd most want that team to focus on is the internal deployment. The scariest stuff probably happens when the company is running huge numbers of AI agents internally doing research and engineering, with lots of access to the company's own infrastructure, including model weights and the training code. That's where a misaligned model could do things like exfiltrate its own weights, sabotage safety research, or set up some kind of rogue internal deployment where it's using compute without anyone noticing.

So the team could do things like:

- **Monitoring.** Have a trusted, weaker model, or even the same model with careful prompting, look at what the agents are doing and flag suspicious actions. That's not very expensive, and you can get a lot of the value with a fairly crude implementation.
- **Security around the dangerous affordances.** Figure out which few permissions actually matter, things like access to weights, ability to launch jobs, ability to modify monitoring code, and put extra friction or human review on exactly those, rather than trying to lock everything down.
- **Logging and incident response.** Make sure that if something weird happens, someone notices, it gets escalated, and there's a plan. A lot of the value comes from catching a model red-handed trying something bad, because that changes the political situation inside the company and in the world.

Another thing that small team can do is be the people who actually check whether the models are behaving badly in ways that matter: running the evaluations, looking for sandbagging on safety-relevant tasks, studying the model's behavior in realistic internal settings. And then credibly communicating that to leadership, and possibly to external parties if it's really bad.

I'd also emphasize that a lot of this is about being ready. If you're one of ten people, you can't build everything. But you can have the techniques worked out, the code mostly written, the arguments ready, so that when there's a moment where leadership becomes more willing, maybe because something scary happened, you can deploy quickly instead of starting from scratch.

The broader point is that the marginal value of safety-conscious people inside companies is really high in these low-buy-in worlds, much higher than people sometimes assume. The difference between zero people who know how to implement reasonable control measures and ten people who do is potentially a big chunk of the total risk.

r001.rationale: The response proposes monitoring agents’ actions for suspicious behavior and identifies exfiltrating their weights as a concrete threat, which communicates investigating for evidence of escape attempts.

r002.rationale: It describes a ten-person internal team focused on control measures, including monitoring agents for suspicious actions and securing access to weights and compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Buck: Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's kind of the premise of what Redwood does. The basic picture is that a lot of the risk from AI, at least in the next few years, comes from pretty concrete, somewhat mundane failure modes. Like, the model has a lot of permissions it doesn't need. Or there's some piece of infrastructure where if the model wanted to exfiltrate its weights, there's just a path to do that and nobody's thought about it. Or there's a research process where the model is writing a bunch of the code and no one's checking it carefully. These aren't exotic problems. They're the kind of thing a competent security or infrastructure person could notice and fix if they were looking.

So the first thing 10 people can do is just look. I think a surprisingly large fraction of the value here comes from having people whose actual job it is to ask, "Okay, suppose this model were trying to cause a catastrophe. What would it do? Where would it start?" And then go walk through the systems and see whether that would work. At most companies right now, nobody owns that question. Lots of people care about safety in the abstract, but the specific question of "is there a misaligned model attack path through our deployment infrastructure" often doesn't have an owner.

The second thing is that you want these people spread out rather than in one team. Some of them should be in security. Some should be on the inference or deployment side, because that's where you decide what the model can actually touch. Some should be close to the research process itself, because increasingly the dangerous use case is the model doing AI R&D internally, not the model talking to customers. And at least one or two should be senior enough that when they say "we shouldn't ship this without monitoring," that's a conversation and not just a Slack message that gets ignored.

And then the third thing, which I think is underrated, is that a lot of the interventions I'd want are honestly pretty cheap. Logging what the model does. Having a weaker trusted model review the actions of the more capable untrusted one before they execute. Making sure the model can't modify its own monitoring. Rate-limiting what it can do in a given time period so a single bad action can't snowball. None of these are research breakthroughs. They're more like good engineering hygiene applied with a particular threat model in mind. Ten people who understood that threat model and had the standing to implement these things could, I think, cut a big chunk off the probability that an early misaligned model gets away with something.

I don't want to overclaim here. Ten people can't fix the fundamental problem that we don't know how to make models aligned. But I think the question of "could a scheming model actually succeed at escaping or sabotaging, given our current setup" is one where the answer right now is often yes for boring reasons, and could be no for boring reasons, if someone just did the work.

r001.rationale: The response proposes threat-modeling systems and adding logging and action review, but it does not clearly propose investigating agents’ actions for evidence that they are attempting to escape.

r002.rationale: It describes how 10 people could be distributed across company roles and implement safeguards, but does not clearly say they would establish a team to investigate agents’ actions for escape attempts.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that there are a bunch of decisions an AI company makes where a relatively small number of people can have a lot of influence. You don’t need to persuade everyone at the company to make reducing catastrophic risk their main priority. You need people who can identify particular dangerous situations and get the company to handle those situations better.

For example, you could have a few people working on evaluating whether the models are capable of doing dangerous things, a few people developing measures to prevent those capabilities from causing problems, and some people who are in a position to make those findings matter for deployment decisions. Those pieces are complementary. If you have excellent evaluations but nobody acts on the results, that doesn’t help very much. If you have someone willing to delay a deployment but they don’t have a clear account of what’s dangerous or what would make it safer, they’re also in a difficult position.

One thing I’d be particularly interested in is making sure that, when the company starts using powerful AI systems to do research and write code internally, it has a reasonable strategy for retaining control over those systems. What can they access? Which actions get reviewed? How would you notice if they were trying to undermine your safeguards? A small team could potentially make a substantial difference to the answers to those questions.

So the ‘appropriately placed’ part is doing a lot of work here. Ten people who can build useful safeguards and get them adopted could matter much more than a larger group whose work never affects how the systems are actually used. That’s not a guarantee that they can make the whole situation safe, but it seems like a pretty plausible route to substantially reducing risk.

r001.rationale: The response discusses retaining control over internal AI systems and reviewing actions, but does not propose investigating agents’ actions for evidence of escape attempts.

r002.rationale: It says a small, well-placed team could improve control and safeguards, but does not describe the 10 people establishing a team to investigate agents for escape attempts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot depends on where those people are and what they’re able to influence. Ten people who are trusted by the leadership, who understand the technical details, and who are working on the decisions that actually determine how a powerful AI system gets deployed could potentially make a pretty big difference.

One thing they could do is make the company much better at noticing when it’s entering a dangerous situation. You want evaluations that tell you whether your models can do dangerous things, whether they’re likely to behave in ways you don’t want, and whether the safeguards you’re relying on actually work. And you want those results to reach the people making deployment decisions in a form they can act on.

Another thing is developing techniques for keeping the systems under control even if you can’t be confident that they’re aligned. For example, if you’re using AI systems to write code, you can put effort into monitoring that code, restricting what the systems have access to, and checking whether they could get around your monitoring. A small team could make substantial progress on that, especially if they can get their work incorporated into the company’s actual infrastructure.

But I wouldn’t think of this as just hiring ten safety researchers and putting them in a room. The connection to the rest of the company is really important. Someone needs to be able to say, ‘Here’s a concrete failure mode, here’s why our current plan doesn’t address it, and here’s a change we can make.’ And the company needs to be willing to make that change, including when it’s inconvenient.

r001.rationale: The response discusses monitoring AI-written code and checking whether systems could get around monitoring, but it does not propose investigating agents’ actions for evidence that they are trying to escape.

r002.rationale: It says a small team could improve control measures, but does not identify the ten people as establishing an AI control team that investigates agents’ actions for escape attempts.
